title: AACS encryption key controversy
text:
In a response to the events occurring on Digg and the call to "Spread this number", the key was rapidly posted to thousands of pages, blogs and wikis across the Internet.[1,2] The reaction was an example of the Streisand effect.[3]

Intellectual property lawyer Douglas J. Sorocco noted, "People are getting creative. It shows the futility of trying to stop this. Once the information is out there, cease-and-desist letters are going to infuriate this community more."[4] Outside the Internet and the mass media, the key has appeared in or on T-shirts, poetry, songs and music videos, illustrations and other graphic artworks,[5] tattoos and body art,[6] and comic strips.[7] The Linux kernel also incorporated a copy of the key for 17.5 years, originally added in 2007 by David Woodhouse as part of the red zone logic[8] and subsequently removed as a routine cleanup in 2024.[9]

On Tuesday afternoon, May 1, 2007, a Google search for the key returned 9,410 results,[10] while the same search the next morning returned nearly 300,000 results.[11] On Friday, the BBC reported that a search on Google shows almost 700,000 pages have published the key,[12] despite the fact that on April 17, the AACS LA sent a DMCA notice to Google, demanding that Google stop returning any results for searches for the key.[13,14]

Widespread news coverage[15,16,17,18,19] included speculation on the development of user-driven websites,[20] the legal liability of running a user-driven website,[21] the perception of acceptance of DRM,[22] the failure as a business model of "secrecy based businesses ... in every aspect" in the Internet era, and the harm an industry can cause itself with harshly-perceived legal action.[23]

In an opposing move, Carter Wood of the National Association of Manufacturers said they had removed the "Digg It" link from their weblog:[24]

> Until the Digg community shows as much fervor in attacking intellectual piracy as attacking the companies that are legitimately defending their property, well, we do not want to be promoting the site by using the "Digg It" feature.

Media coverage initially avoided quoting the key itself. However, several US-based news sources have run stories containing the key, quoting its use on Digg,[25,26,27,28,29,30]

though none are known to have received DMCA notices as a result. Later reports have discussed this, quoting the key.[31] Current TV broadcast the key during a Google Current story on the Digg incident on May 3, 2007, displaying it in full on screen for several seconds and placing the story on the station website.[32]

On May 1, 2007, Wikipedia locked out the page named for the number "to prevent the former secret from being posted again". The page on HD DVD was locked as well, to keep out "The Number".[33] This action was later reversed. No one has been arrested or charged for finding or publishing the original key.[34]

### AACS LA reaction

On May 7, 2007, the AACS LA announced on its website that it had "requested the removal solely of illegal circumvention tools, including encryption keys, from a number of web sites", and that it had "not requested the removal or deletion of any ... discussion or commentary". The statement continued, "AACS LA is encouraged by the cooperation it has received thus far from the numerous web sites that have chosen to address their legal obligations in a responsible manner."[35] BBC News had earlier quoted an AACS executive saying that bloggers "crossed the line", that AACS was looking at "legal and technical tools" to confront those who published the key, and that the events involving Digg were an "interesting new twist".[12]
